prompt:
Research what the Rust project officially documents about its release cadence and how long each stable version is supported. Cite the official Rust page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
The Rust project officially documents that its release cadence follows a six-week schedule based on a "release train" model, and that each stable version is supported for exactly six weeks (until the next stable version is released, at which point the previous version reaches end-of-life).

SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html | QUOTE: "Rust releases every six weeks, like clockwork." | CLAIM: The official release cadence for stable Rust versions is every six weeks.
SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html | QUOTE: "When a new stable version is released, the old version reaches its end of life (EOL). This means each version is supported for six weeks." | CLAIM: Each stable version of Rust is supported for six weeks.
SOURCE: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/0507-release-channels.html | QUOTE: "Development cycles are reduced to six weeks from the current twelve." | CLAIM: The release train model cycles are six weeks long.
SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/index.html | QUOTE: "Rust has a new language release every six weeks." | CLAIM: The Rust language releases on a six-week cadence.
